paper_summary: The paper introduces GRADINO, a configurable, from-scratch generator and benchmark framework for numerical question answering (QA) over multiple non-relational (visually/pivoted/perturbed) tables. GRADINO synthesizes a latent relational source (schema + dense data), uses executable SQL over that latent source to produce gold answers (aggregation-style: SUM/AVG/MAX/MIN), and then renders answer-preserving perturbations to produce non-relational views (pivots/hierarchical headers/merged cells, OCR noise, nulls, unit changes, etc.). It supports two multi-table evidence-flow topologies: parallel (independent scalar per view then aggregate) and sequential (lookup chains where intermediate results are propagated). An LLM verbalizes SQL queries into NL questions and a verifier repairs inconsistent verbalizations. The authors evaluate multiple LLMs (gpt-5-mini and several Qwen variants) across financial and environmental domains, sweeping table counts (2..20), unit heterogeneity, and perturbations. Key findings are a sharp, compound degradation in performance as table count grows (esp. for quantitative questions), large sensitivity to unit heterogeneity (domain dependent), and that GRADINO-generated training data can improve fine-tuned models and complement scarce real multi-table training data. The paper releases prompts, generation details, code, and generated datasets.
summary_of_strengths: 1) Novel evaluation generator: GRADINO fills a clear gap by enabling controlled, verifiable evaluation of multi-table QA under realistic non-relational renderings while preserving gold answers via a latent SQL source. 2) Clear conceptual contribution: separating supervision (latent SQL) from presentation (perturbed, non-relational views) is principled and enables systematic ablations across table count, layout, and unit axes. 3) Thorough empirical study: the paper shows consistent, substantive failure modes (scaling collapse, unit heterogeneity, sequential vs parallel differences) across multiple models and two domains, and validates degradation on perturbed real tables. 4) Practical value: GRADINO-generated data improves fine-tuning on a scarce in-domain benchmark (GRI-QA) and complements real datasets. 5) Reproducibility effort: the paper provides prompts, generation details, hyperparameters, manual verification statistics, and commits to releasing code and datasets.
summary_of_weaknesses: 1) Synthetic realism gap: GRADINO is a diagnostic generator and does not fully replicate all distributional, visual, and semantic complexities of real-world spreadsheets/reports (authors acknowledge this). This limits immediate claims about real-world deployability. 2) Restricted reasoning patterns: focus is on numeric aggregation-style questions with a single distinguished numeric column and two topologies (parallel/sequential with unique matches). More general multi-table joins, set operations, or tree-shaped/semi-ambiguous joins are not explored. 3) Question-verbalization fragility: NL questions are produced by an LLM and, while verification and manual checks show high fidelity overall, sequential questions are notably more error-prone (authors report ~92.5% correctness) which could affect downstream evaluation if not curated. 4) Dependence on internal LLM and prompt-engineering: the generation pipeline uses an LLM (gpt-5-mini) to produce schemas and constraints; this may introduce generation biases and reduces deterministic reproducibility for users without access to the same model. 5) Limited perturbation modalities: some real-world cues (visual alignment, charts, more complex layout/formatting) are not modeled; results therefore may under- or over-estimate failures on more visually rich documents.
comments_suggestions_typos: - The paper is well-written and the appendix is thorough (prompts, constraints, solver details). A few suggestions: (a) expand discussion or experiments on multi-match / ambiguous-key sequential scenarios (tree-shaped joins), even if sampled sparsely, to assess generality; (b) provide ablations on the effect of different kinds of unit conversions (non-linear, percent vs absolute) and conversion difficulty; (c) clarify in the main text how many generated candidates are discarded in each regime and the resulting selection bias (appendix has details, but a short summary in the main paper would help); (d) consider adding an evaluation with more publicly-available LLMs (for reproducibility) or report sensitivity when swapping the internal generation LLM; (e) a short checklist for practitioners explaining when GRADINO instances should vs should not be taken as realistic would help. I found no substantive typos that hinder comprehension.
limitations_and_societal_impact: The authors explicitly discuss limitations (synthetic realism, restricted numerical focus) and ethical considerations (synthetic fictional entities, public sources for validation, licenses). They note that strong performance on GRADINO should not be taken as a guarantee of real-world reliability. Missing/expandable points: (1) potential domain and language coverage gaps — GRADINO is demonstrated on finance and environmental domains but may behave differently for other domains or languages; (2) LLM-induced lexical biases — schema/lexicon generated by a particular LLM may reflect its training data and introduce subtle distributional artifacts; (3) downstream risk: silent numeric errors in deployed systems can have real consequences, and guidance for safe deployment/testing using GRADINO would be useful. Overall, the treatment of limitations and impact is responsible but could be amplified with more concrete deployment guidance.
ethical_concerns: No major ACL Code of Ethics violations. Data generation uses synthetic fictional entities so privacy concerns are minimal; real tables used for validation are public and appropriately cited. One minor concern is reliance on internally hosted/closed models (gpt-5-mini) during generation which could embed proprietary biases into the benchmarks—authors should encourage/enable reproductions with open models. The paper reports the licenses of used artifacts. Overall ethical handling is adequate.
